title: A Vision for Robust and Human-Centric LLM-Based QR Code Security
authors: Hissah Almousa; Ellis Solaiman
abstract: Quick Response (QR) codes are now widely used as a digital communication tool. However, their extensive adoption has made them an attractive target for cyberattacks, particularly through the injection of malicious URLs that redirect users to phishing sites or initiate malware installations. Conventional security approaches such as blacklists and antivirus software are no longer efficient against such evolving threats. This vision paper proposes an AI-based framework using fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify malicious URLs embedded within QR codes. To ensure transparency, a novel ensemble Explainable AI (XAI) is applied to aggregate insights from various XAI methods to explain the features influencing model predictions, facilitating more robust interpretations. To enhance clarity and usability, the proposed framework incorporates personalized explanations tailored to cybersecurity analysts, system developers, and non-expert end users, informed by a role-specific user study. Furthermore, as XAI methods may expose sensitive model behavior, cyberattackers craft adversarial inputs to mislead the model or manipulate explanations. This necessitates the integration of adversarial training to ensure model robustness and explanation integrity, evaluated through perturbation consistency checks. The paper outlines key challenges in explanation fidelity and personalization and presents a development roadmap to advance secure, transparent, and human-centric explainable QR code analysis.

title: Auditing Synthetic Code: A Multi-Dimensional Taxonomy and Evaluation Framework for LLM-Generated Code Training Data
authors: Matin Rouzehkhah Azad
abstract: Background: LLM-generated synthetic code is now a standard ingredient in code-LM training, but its quality is rarely audited before entering the fine-tune loop. The de facto n-gram contamination check over-flags universal boilerplate and under-flags problem-level paraphrase, and the literature lacks a structured measurement scaffold to take its place.Methods: We propose an audit taxonomy with operational framework for LLM-generated synthetic code, mapped to ISO/IEC 25010 software-quality characteristics. The taxonomy organises nine dimensions into three operational bands (contamination, structural-and-semantic, execution), embeds a rule-based two-axis contamination diagnostic with four operationally distinct cells, and is exposed through a deterministic open-source Python implementation. We apply the audit taxonomy to five public synthetic-code datasets and validate it downstream by LoRA-fine-tuning code-LMs across three Qwen-Coder sizes, StarCoder2-3B, and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B on MBPP-500 and HumanEval.Results: Four strong-signal axes discriminate the datasets at medium-to-large multi-seed effect sizes (Friedman p <= 0.0012 on every strong axis). A uniform-weight five-axis composite rank-orders the five datasets against MBPP-500 pass@1 within the Qwen-Coder family (Spearman rho >= +0.70); cross-family transfer is partial on StarCoder2-3B (rho = +0.60) and does not hold on DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B (rho = -0.20). HumanEval inverts the ordering, showing benchmark-contingent predictivity.Conclusions: The audit taxonomy discriminates synthetic-code datasets consistently and supplies a reusable knowledge artefact for synthetic-data quality assurance. Downstream predictivity is family- and benchmark-contingent; we report it as bounded validation evidence rather than a general predictivity claim.

title: Security Knowledge Distillation for Enhancing LLM Safety in Code Generation Authors
authors: Sarah Mitchell; Jason Li; Daniel Thompson
abstract: We propose a distillation framework that transfers secure coding expertise into a compact model trained using expert demonstrations, static-analysis labels, and secure patterns. The distilled model (7B parameters) achieves 83% security compliance, nearly matching GPT-4's 89% performance while requiring significantly less compute. Evaluated across CWE-20, CWE-78, CWE-89, the distilled model reduces injection vulnerabilities by 62% relative to baseline models. This work demonstrates that targeted distillation can teach smaller models to respect security best practices.

title: Security Unit Test Generation for LLM-Produced Code Using Constraint-Based Mutation Authors
authors: Sophie Maes; Jonas De Wilde; Liam Verhoeven
abstract: We propose an automated unit test generator designed to reveal security weaknesses in LLM-generated programs. The system applies constraint-based input mutation combined with vulnerability oracles for injection, overflow, and authentication flaws. Evaluated on 1,500 code samples generated by five LLMs, the framework detects 41% more security faults than fuzzing-based test generators. Code coverage increases by 22%, and time-to-bug discovery is reduced by half. The results show the value of pairing LLM outputs with adversarial unit-test synthesis.

title: Security Weaknesses in LLM-Generated Source Code: An Empirical Vulnerability Analysis of Iterative AI-Assisted Development
authors: Halil Dursunoglu; Kaan Sulkalar
abstract: Context: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineeringworkflows for code generation, debugging, refactoring, and feature development. While previousresearch has examined the security of one-shot code generation, the longitudinal impact of iterativeAI-assisted software refinement on software security remains insufficiently understood.Objective: This study investigates how software vulnerabilities evolve throughout iterative AI-assisted development workflows and introduces a framework for measuring security degradationduring conversational software refinement.Method: We propose SecureIterate, a longitudinal evaluation framework that combines promptorchestration, version tracking, static analysis, runtime validation, fuzz testing, and CWE/OWASP-based vulnerability normalization. Using 1,250 generated software versions spanning multiple pro-gramming languages, application categories, and commercial and open-source LLM families, weevaluate vulnerability propagation across repeated refinement stages. Security Drift Score (SDS) andWeighted Security Drift Score (WSDS) are introduced to quantify longitudinal security changes.Results: The experimental results reveal statistically significant vulnerability growth throughoutiterative refinement cycles. Common weaknesses included SQL injection, improper authentication,hardcoded credentials, path traversal, insecure deserialization, and unsafe dependency usage. Cross-model analysis showed that vulnerability propagation occurred across all evaluated LLM families.Runtime validation and fuzz testing identified additional security issues not detected through staticanalysis alone. Security-aware prompting, static-analysis-guided refinement, and dependency verifi-cation reduced vulnerability growth and improved security outcomes.Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that iterative AI-assisted software development can introducemeasurable security drift despite functional improvements. SecureIterate provides a reproducibleframework for evaluating longitudinal software security and highlights the importance of continuoussecurity validation, automated assurance mechanisms, and human oversight in AI-assisted softwareengineering workflows.

title: Enhancing Code Security Specification Detection in Software Development with LLM
authors: Shanqi Zhan; Ying Lin; Yao Yao; Junlin Zhu
abstract: In order to improve the accuracy and efficiency of code security specification detection in the software development process, a large-scale language model (LLM)-based detection architecture is constructed to realize deep semantic parsing and structured rule matching for high-complexity code in multilingual environments. The research designs a security specification controlled language system integrating CFG and AST, covering 62 rule items, 480 types of semantic labels and 3000 AST nodes, and introduces a quintuple language model G = (N, Σ, P, S, C) to construct five types of key constraint domains, including variable naming, privilege boundaries, input validation and so on. The structural semantic graph with 2.1×10⁶ edges is constructed by graph neural network, and a deep detection model containing 690 million parameters is designed to support sliding window scanning and semantic embedding matching, adapting to 45 kinds of security constraint structures. The experiments are tested in 1.38 million function fragments, and the detection accuracy is more than 93%, among which the accuracy of memory access out-of-bounds class reaches 95.6%, which verifies the high adaptability and stability of the model in the aspects of function privilege control, input validation and memory security.

title: ASG-LLM: An LLM-Based Pipeline for Automated Scraping Code Generation in Security-Sensitive Environments
authors: Sokheang Chan; Naro Vorn; Vungsovanreach Kong; Chang Kue Seok; Jong-Hyun Kim; Dr. Anand Nayyar; Tae-Kyung KIM
abstract: Automating interactions with security-sensitive web services remains difficult due to dynamic frontends, session-bound tokens, and undocumented parameter-generation logic. Traditionally, developers must manually analyze captured traffic, hypothesize parameter-generation routines, and iteratively test internally defined functions until the interaction succeeds. We propose ASG-LLM, an execution grounded pipeline that generates scraping modules from a single successful browser session trace. ASG-LLM captures full HTTP(S) traffic, removes irrelevant requests through multi-stage filtering, and constructs a dependency-aware representation of the core interaction flow. When security-critical parameters cannot be reconstructed from the trace alone, the FUNC Retriever identifies a small set of reusable internal function descriptions using HyDE-guided selective retrieval, enabling the LLM to select compatible parameter-generation routines based on behavioral similarity rather than keyword matching, without exposing proprietary implementation code. Generated modules are executed in a controlled environment and iteratively repaired using structured failure feedback. ASG-LLM was evaluated on representative banking and public-sector portals. In our case studies, ASG-LLM reduces developer effort by cutting traffic analysis and basic code implementation from hours to minutes and reducing security-handling effort from a full-day task to a couple of hours. At the model level, HyDE-based selective retrieval improves internal function recommendation accuracy from 30% to 70% Top-1 and from 60% to 90% Top-3 compared with a full-context baseline. These results suggest that combining trace grounding, selective retrieval, and execution-time validation is a promising direction for robust web automation in security-constrained environments.

title: Evaluating Security and Inclusivity in LLM-Generated Code: A Controlled Experiment
authors: Bilal Naqvi; Waleed  Bin Shahid; Janne Parkkila; AKM Bahalul Haque; Hammad Afzal
abstract: Despite developments in the human aspects of cybersecurity, inclusivity concerns, particularly related to neurodiversity, remain largely unexplored. One reason for this gap is a limited understanding among practitioners concerning inclusivity and neurodiversity. This paper examines the role that Large Language Models (LLMs) can play in generating code that integrates inclusivity concerns in the development of security systems and services. A controlled experiment was conducted with three experimental cases, constructed by varying the level of inclusivity specification from no specification in the first case to a detailed specification in the third. Moreover, after each round, the LLM-generated code artifact was evaluated against security and inclusivity criteria by 13 human experts and five LLM-based reviewers using a rubric-based assessment. The results demonstrate that an increase in the specification detail improves the inclusivity of LLM-generated code without causing any negative impact (trade-offs) on security. Statistical comparisons using Welch’s independentsamples t-tests revealed no statistically significant difference between human and LLM-based evaluations for inclusivity, whereas a significant difference was observed for security assessments. Effect size analysis (Cohen’s d) indicated a substantial divergence in security evaluation patterns between humans and LLM evaluators. The findings have implications for (i) research in terms of advancing the state of the art concerning integration of LLMs in the phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC), secure software engineering, and (ii) practice in terms of the role of specification details, and complementary strengths between human and LLM evaluators to support evaluation of LLM-generated code.
